items.title: Iranian missile partially collapses Haifa building, injuring at least 10

featured_image.name: Israel Says Haifa Residential Building Suffers Direct Hit in Iran Attack

items.description: An Iranian ballistic missile slammed into a residential building in the northern Israeli city of Haifa on Sunday, partially collapsing the structure and injuring at least four people as rescue teams scrambled to search for others potentially trapped beneath the rubble. The strike marks one of the most damaging single hits on Israeli civilian infrastructure since the war between the U.S.-Israel coalition and Iran entered its sixth week.

items.title: US rescues downed airman in Iran as energy strike deadline looms

featured_image.name: US fighter jet shot down over Iran, one crew member rescued ... - Axios

items.description: The war between the United States, Israel, and Iran entered its sixth week on Sunday with no ceasefire in sight, as a dramatic rescue of a downed American airman, continued Iranian missile barrages on Israeli cities, and an approaching deadline on strikes against Iranian energy infrastructure converged to deepen the crisis.

items.title: Trump threatens to bomb Iran's power plants after downed airman's rescue

featured_image.name: Trump issues 48-hour Hormuz Strait ultimatum, threatens Iran’s power plants

items.description: An American airman shot down over Iran was rescued early Sunday in what President Trump called "one of the most daring Search and Rescue Operations in US History," capping a harrowing two-day race between U.S. special operations forces and Iranian troops hunting for the downed crew member as the six-week-old war entered its most volatile phase yet.

items.title: Iran launches Wave 96 strikes on Israel and Gulf energy sites

featured_image.name: Israel targets Iranian missile crews as Haifa's historic mosque damaged in  strike

items.description:
Iran launched a sweeping barrage of missiles and drones targeting Israel and energy infrastructure across the Persian Gulf on Sunday, marking the 37th day of the war that began when the United States and Israel struck Iran on February 28. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said the attacks, designated Wave 96 of Operation True Promise 4, were retaliation for U.S.-Israeli strikes on a bridge in Karaj and petrochemical facilities in Mahshahr.[1][2][3][4]

An Iranian ballistic missile scored a direct hit on a seven-story residential building in the northern Israeli city of Haifa, injuring four people, the Israeli military and Magen David Adom emergency service confirmed to AFP. Among the wounded was an 82-year-old man in serious condition who was pulled from the rubble after being struck by heavy debris. Images published by medics showed smoke rising from the flattened remains of the building in a densely populated area.[5][6][7]

Separately, an Iranian missile struck the Neot Hovav industrial complex near Beersheba in southern Israel, according to Israeli army radio. The site, one of Israel's largest chemical manufacturing zones, has been hit repeatedly during the conflict, with previous strikes in late March triggering fires and hazardous material concerns.[8][9][10]

items.title: Iran surpasses 500 ballistic missiles fired at Israel in five-week war

featured_image.name: Iran's use of cluster munitions against Israel may be a war crime

items.description: More than 500 ballistic missiles have been launched from Iran at Israel since the start of the war on February 28, the Times of Israel reported Sunday, as the conflict entered its 37th day with no ceasefire in sight. Roughly half of those missiles have carried cluster munition warheads, according to the Israel Defense Forces, a tactic that has exposed vulnerabilities in Israel's layered air defense systems and killed at least four civilians in documented strikes.[1][2][3]

items.title: Polymer prices surge over 40% as Iran war chokes global supply

featured_image.name: Iran could disrupt the Strait of Hormuz with drones for months | Reuters

items.description:
Five weeks into the U.S.-Israel war with Iran, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz is rippling far beyond oil markets, triggering a crisis in global plastics and petrochemicals that is pushing up prices for everyday goods from bottled water to food packaging.

Polymer prices have surged roughly 41 to 42 percent since hostilities erupted on February 28, according to industry tracker Polymer Update, with some segments such as PVC in India climbing as much as 78 percent. The disruption has proven stubbornly persistent: even as crude oil corrected from its peak above $126 per barrel, polymer prices have continued to climb as physical supply shortages deepen across Asia and Europe.[1][2]

items.title: Iran launches missiles at Israel, Kuwait after rejecting Trump ultimatum

featured_image.name: Iranian missiles seen over Hebron

items.description: Iran launched missiles and drones at Israel and Kuwait early Sunday, hours after its military command rejected President Donald Trump's ultimatum to reach a peace deal within 48 hours or face devastating strikes on its vital infrastructure. Both Kuwait and Israel said their air defense systems were activated to respond to the latest barrage, extending a conflict now in its sixth week.[1][2][3][4]

items.title: Moody's cuts India growth forecast as Hormuz oil crisis widens

featured_image.name: The economy has Strait of Hormuz deadline for Trump: Two weeks

items.description: The closure of the Strait of Hormuz, now in its fifth week, is sending widening economic shockwaves far beyond the Middle East, with the spot price of Brent crude soaring to $141.36 per barrel on April 2 — the highest level since the 2008 financial crisis — as governments from Seoul to Dakar scramble to contain the fallout.[1][2]

items.title: Artemis II crew nears Moon despite recurring toilet problems

featured_image.name: NASA Answers Your Most Pressing Artemis II Questions

items.description: Four days into humanity's first crewed lunar voyage in more than half a century, the Artemis II astronauts have been plagued by recurring problems with their $23 million space toilet — a device NASA spent six years developing and that was supposed to represent a leap forward in deep-space hygiene.

items.title: Putin's approval hits lowest point since Ukraine invasion

featured_image.name: Russia is restricting access to Telegram, one of its most popular ...

items.description:
Vladimir Putin's approval rating has fallen to its lowest point since the eve of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, as public anger mounts over the Kremlin's decision to restrict and ultimately block Telegram, the country's most widely used messaging platform.

Data from Russia's Public Opinion Foundation (FOM), published in early April by The Moscow Times, shows trust in Putin fell five percentage points in a single week — from 76% to 71% — in a survey conducted between March 27 and 29. It marks the sharpest weekly decline the pollster has recorded since at least 2019. Figures from the state-run Russian Public Opinion Research Center (VTsIOM) corroborate the trend, showing Putin's approval at 70.1% while disapproval rose from 14.8% in January to 18.3% in March.[1][2]

items.title: Taiwan's KMT leader set to visit China Tuesday for first such trip in a decade

featured_image.name: Taiwan opposition leader to make 'peace' visit to China - Global News

items.description:
Taiwan's main opposition leader Cheng Li-wun is set to travel to China on Tuesday for a six-day visit, becoming the first sitting Kuomintang chairperson to make the trip in a decade. Cheng, who accepted an invitation from Chinese President Xi Jinping and the Central Committee of the Communist Party of China, will lead a KMT delegation to Jiangsu, Shanghai, and Beijing from April 7 to 12, weeks before U.S. President Donald Trump's own anticipated visit to Beijing in mid-May.[1][2][3]

Cheng has said she wants to meet Xi to build cross-strait "peace" and show the world that the two sides "are not destined for war". China's official Xinhua News Agency confirmed the invitation but has not specified whether a meeting with Xi is formally on the agenda. Cheng is expected to visit Sun Yat-sen's Mausoleum in Nanjing on April 8, though few other details have been released.[4][2][5][6]

items.title: Trump says US sent guns to Iranian protesters via Kurds

featured_image.name: What you need to know: 5 key takeaways from Trump's Iran address

items.description:
President Donald Trump publicly acknowledged on Sunday that the United States had sent weapons to anti-regime protesters in Iran earlier this year, disclosing that the arms were funneled through Kurdish militia forces — but suggesting the effort failed because the Kurds kept the guns for themselves.

"We sent guns to the protesters, a lot of them. We sent them to the Kurds," Trump told Fox News in a phone interview on April 5. "And I think the Kurds took the guns."[1][2]

The admission marks the first time a sitting president has publicly confirmed direct U.S. material support for Iran's domestic opposition during the ongoing conflict, which began with the launch of Operation Epic Fury on February 28.[3]

items.title: Trump gives Iran 48 hours as oil crisis deepens

featured_image.name: Trump threatens Iran with "hell" if Hormuz strait isn't open in 48 hours

items.description:
President Donald Trump issued a 48-hour ultimatum to Iran on Saturday, warning on Truth Social that "all Hell will reign down on them" if Tehran does not reopen the Strait of Hormuz or agree to a deal, escalating a crisis that has already sent crude oil prices to levels not seen in years and shaken financial markets worldwide.[1][2]

The ultimatum, the second such deadline Trump has imposed since mid-March, came as WTI crude oil futures settled at $111.54 per barrel on April 2 after surging more than 11% in a single session, according to EFE. Brent crude traded near $109 the same day. The spike followed Trump's televised address on April 1 in which he vowed to strike Iran "extremely hard" and offered no exit ramp from the conflict, dashing market hopes for a swift de-escalation, CNBC reported.[3][4][5]

items.title: OPEC+ warns Gulf energy repairs will take years

featured_image.name: OPEC+ set to hold monitoring meeting in early February | Reuters

items.description:
OPEC+'s Joint Ministerial Monitoring Committee raised alarm on Sunday over the mounting damage to energy facilities across the Gulf, warning that restoring infrastructure to full capacity "is both costly and takes a long time" and poses a direct threat to global supply.[1]

The 65th JMMC meeting, held by videoconference, brought together ministers from Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, the UAE, Kuwait, Kazakhstan, Nigeria, Algeria, and Venezuela to assess what the International Energy Agency has called "the largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market".[2][3]

items.title: Slovak PM calls EU a 'suicide ship,' demands end to Russia sanctions

featured_image.name: Slovakia to allow approval of new EU sanctions on Russia on ...

items.description: Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico on Saturday called the European Union a "suicide ship" on energy security, demanding the bloc lift sanctions on Russian oil and gas as Europe grapples with soaring fuel costs driven by the war in Iran. The broadside, delivered after a phone call with Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, marks the sharpest challenge yet to EU unity on Russia sanctions amid a worsening energy emergency.

items.title: Iran urges UN action over nuclear site strikes, warns of radioactive fallout

featured_image.name: Projectile hits near Iran’s Bushehr nuclear plant, killing one: IAEA

items.description: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi sent urgent letters on Saturday to UN Secretary-General António Guterres, the UN Security Council, and International Atomic Energy Agency Director-General Rafael Grossi, warning that repeated U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran's nuclear facilities risk spreading radioactive contamination across the Gulf region.[1][2][3]

items.title: Bitcoin trades flat as Trump's Iran deadline nears Monday

featured_image.name: Trump issues 48-hour Hormuz Strait ultimatum, threatens Iran's ...

items.description: Bitcoin traded in a narrow range between $66,500 and $67,300 on Sunday as crypto markets held their breath ahead of President Trump's April 6 deadline for Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. The ultimatum, posted to Truth Social on Saturday, warned that "all Hell will reign down" on Iran if it fails to comply, setting up a potentially volatile start to the week for risk assets.[1][2][3]

items.title: Japan bond yields hit 25-year high, stoking carry trade fears

featured_image.name: Japan 10 Year Government Bond Yield - Quote - Chart - Historical Data - News

items.description: Japanese government bond yields have surged to their highest levels in more than a quarter century, intensifying fears that a structural shift in Japan's monetary landscape could drain a vital source of global liquidity. The benchmark 10-year yield touched 2.393% in early April, a level not seen since 1999, as markets price in growing odds of another Bank of Japan rate hike later this month.[1][2][3]

items.title: IMF urges BOJ rate hike as oil shock reshapes global monetary policy

featured_image.name: Bank of Japan chief stresses need to hit 2% inflation backed by wage gains  | Reuters

items.description:
The US-Israel-Iran conflict has upended the trajectory of global monetary policy, forcing central banks from Frankfurt to Tokyo to Cairo to shelve plans for easing and brace for a potential return to rate hikes as surging oil prices reignite inflation across the world economy.

Brent crude has risen more than 50% since late February, with spot prices hitting $141 per barrel on April 2 — the highest since 2008 — while futures have traded around $112 in recent days. The spike, driven largely by disruptions to the Strait of Hormuz, has sent shockwaves through inflation data and central bank boardrooms alike.[1][2]

items.title: China, Russia align to block force in Hormuz resolution

featured_image.name: High stakes in the Strait of Hormuz: Force majeure and supply chain ...

items.description: The United Nations Security Council is expected to vote next week on a Bahraini resolution aimed at protecting commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, more than a month after Iran effectively closed the critical waterway in the wake of joint U.S.-Israeli military strikes. The vote, originally scheduled for April 3 and then April 4, was postponed amid deep divisions among the council's permanent members over language authorizing the use of force.[1][2][3][4]
